sections.title: The Privacy Paradox
sections.content: Introduction to the challenge of contact tracing: How can we track exposure to a virus without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state? Contrast the Centralized model (where a server knows everyone's location) with the Decentralized (DP-3T) model.
sections.example: Imagine two animals, Pip the Penguin and Leo the Lion, passing each other in a forest. They want to be able to warn each other if they get sick later, but they don't want a 'Forest King' server to know exactly when or where they met.

sections.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions
sections.content: Explanation of cryptographic hashing and seeds. Visualizing a 'Secret Shaker': you put a secret key in, and it generates a unique, unpredictable string of numbers. Crucially, you can't go backwards from the numbers to the key.
sections.example: A mathematical 'blender' icon: Inputting a 'Seed of the Day' produces a sequence of 'Rolling Codes' that look like random noise to anyone watching.

sections.title: The Daily Secret & Rolling IDs
sections.content: Every day, Pip’s phone generates a 'Secret Day Key' (SKt). From this key, the phone derives 'Rolling Proximity Identifiers' (RPIs) that change every 15 minutes. This prevents someone from tracking Pip throughout the day using a static ID.
sections.example: Pip’s phone broadcasts 'A12B' at 10:00 AM and 'C99X' at 10:15 AM. To Leo, these look like two completely different strangers.

sections.title: The Digital Handshake (Log Storage)
sections.content: When Pip and Leo are close, their phones exchange these RPIs via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE). Each phone stores the IDs it *hears* in a local, encrypted 'Diary' folder. No location data (GPS) is ever recorded.
sections.example: Leo’s phone 'hears' Pip's RPI and whispers to its internal storage: 'I saw code A12B today at a signal strength of -70dB.' Leo’s phone doesn't know this code belongs to Pip.

sections.title: Sounding the Alarm: The Diagnosis Upload
sections.content: If Pip tests positive, he uploads his 'Secret Day Keys' for the last 14 days to a central server. Note: He does NOT upload his contacts. The server only hosts a list of 'Sick Keys'—not identities.
sections.example: Pip sends his 'Secret Day Key' (the seed) to a public bulletin board. The board shows: 'The owner of the seed that produced these codes is sick,' but the board doesn't know who Pip met.

sections.title: Local Matching: The Private Detective
sections.content: Every phone periodically downloads the new 'Sick Keys' from the server. Leo's phone uses these keys to recreate all possible RPIs that the sick person *would* have broadcasted. It then compares these to the codes in its local 'Diary'.
sections.example: Leo's phone runs the 'Secret Shaker' math on Pip's uploaded key. It generates 'A12B'. It checks the Diary, finds 'A12B', and alerts Leo: 'You were near someone who is now sick!'

sections.title: Summary: Privacy by Design
sections.content: Recap of why DP-3T is secure: 1. Identities stay on devices. 2. The server never sees the 'Handshake'. 3. All matching happens locally. The math ensures that even the government can't reconstruct the social graph.
sections.example: A split-screen visual: On the left, a Centralized 'Web' connecting everyone. On the right, DP-3T shows isolated dots that only connect momentarily on their own terms.

storyboard.title: The Privacy Paradox
lecture_lines: Digital contact tracing helps slow virus spread.
Centralized models risk creating a surveillance state.
DP-3T balances public health with individual privacy.
animations: Pip (Penguin) and Leo (Lion) icons appear at LEFT and RIGHT of the screen.
A server icon labeled 'Forest King' (#FF4444) appears in the center.
Pip and Leo move toward each other; lines connect both to the central server.
The server and lines fade out; Pip and Leo are enclosed in green 'Private' circles (#00FF00).
The text 'DP-3T: Privacy-First' appears in the center (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: One-Way Hash Functions
lecture_lines: Cryptographic hashing turns inputs into unique strings.
These one-way functions cannot be reversed.
A secret seed generates unpredictable rolling codes.
animations: A blender icon labeled 'Hash Function' (#FFFFFF) appears in the center.
A yellow 'Seed' block (#FFFF00) enters the blender; green 'Rolling Codes' (#00FF00) flow out.
A red 'One-Way' arrow (#FF0000) appears, indicating the process cannot be reversed.

storyboard.title: The Daily Secret & Rolling IDs
lecture_lines: Each day, phones generate a new Secret Day Key.
This key derives Rolling Proximity Identifiers every fifteen minutes.
Frequent rotation prevents tracking by malicious observers.
To others, Pip's ID looks like a total stranger.
animations: Pip's phone icon is shown containing a 'Secret Day Key' (#FFA500).
A code 'A12B' (#00FFFF) pulses from the phone with a '10:00 AM' timestamp.
The code 'A12B' changes to 'C99X' (#00FFFF) with a '10:15 AM' timestamp.

storyboard.title: The Digital Handshake (Log Storage)
lecture_lines: Nearby phones exchange rolling IDs via Bluetooth.
Observed codes are stored in a local, encrypted diary.
No location data or identities are ever recorded.
animations: Pip and Leo's phones pulse with light blue Bluetooth waves (#ADD8E6) as they pass each other.
Leo's phone displays a folder icon labeled 'Local Diary' (#90EE90).
The code 'A12B' moves from Pip's phone into Leo's 'Local Diary' folder.

storyboard.title: Sounding the Alarm: The Diagnosis Upload
lecture_lines: If Pip tests positive, he uploads his daily keys.
He never uploads his contact diary or identity.
The server only stores keys of infected users.
Only Pip's secret seeds are made public.
animations: Pip's phone turns red (#FF0000) and displays a 'Positive Test' icon.
Pip's 'Secret Day Keys' (#FFA500) fly from his phone to a 'Public Bulletin Board' (#FFFFFF).
The Bulletin Board displays the keys with a label 'Anonymous Sick Keys'.
A green 'Privacy Shield' (#00FF00) appears over Pip's identity on his device.
The text 'No Personal Data Uploaded' flashes on the screen (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Local Matching: The Private Detective
lecture_lines: Phones download the list of daily sick keys.
Leo's phone recreates RPIs from these uploaded keys.
Matching codes in the local diary triggers an alert.
animations: Leo's phone downloads the 'Secret Day Keys' (#FFA500) from the Public Bulletin Board.
Leo's phone processes the key to recreate the code 'A12B' (#00FFFF).
A magnifying glass (#FFFFFF) scans the 'Local Diary' and finds the matching 'A12B'.
The matching code in the diary flashes yellow (#FFFF00) to indicate a hit.
A red 'Exposure Warning' banner (#FF0000) appears on Leo's phone screen.

storyboard.title: Summary: Privacy by Design
lecture_lines: DP-3T ensures matching happens only on your device.
The server never learns who met whom.
Cryptography secures health data against surveillance.
animations: A split screen shows a red Centralized web (#FF4444) vs green Decentralized dots (#00FF00).
Lock icons (#FFD700) appear on all phone-to-phone digital handshakes.
The text 'Privacy by Design' scales up and glows in the center (#00FF00).
